title: Servo Dial
intro: Turn a knob and a servo motor follows it, like a dial on a dashboard.

wiring_steps.title: The knob
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Push the potentiometer in so its two outside legs go in E8 and E10 and its middle leg in G9. Add a black wire from A8 to the blue (−) rail, a red wire from A10 to the red (+) rail, and a wire from {{pin:POT_PIN}} to J9 (the middle leg).

wiring_steps.title: The servo
wiring_steps.text: Plug three wires into the servo's plug. Brown (or black) goes to the blue (−) rail, orange (or yellow) goes to {{pin:SERVO_PIN}}, and red is power. This part needs 5V. On a 5V board (Uno, Nano, Mega) it uses the red (+) rail. On an ESP board the rail is only 3.3V, so its red wire goes straight to {{5V}} on the board.

steps.title: Read the knob
steps.text:
A potentiometer (pot) is a knob that changes a voltage as you turn it. `analogRead(POT_PIN)` turns it into a number from 0 up to `ANALOG_MAX`.

**Your task:** Run the code, open the **Serial Monitor**, and turn the knob all the way each way.
hints: In the simulator, drag the knob on the potentiometer.
Turn it fully one way for the smallest number, and fully the other way for the biggest.
Try the Serial Plotter tab for a graph.

checks.label: Turned the other way: a big number
The number changes when I turn the knob

steps.success: Your knob works. It gives a whole range of numbers: that's an analog input.

steps.title: Test the servo
steps.text:
A servo is a motor that turns to the angle you ask for, from 0° to 180°. The **Servo** library does the hard work: `attach` connects it to a pin and `write(90)` turns it to 90°.

**Your task:** fill in the blank so the servo turns to 180°, then Run.
steps.success: The servo works. 0°, 90°, 180°: it goes exactly where you tell it.

steps.title: The knob turns the servo
steps.text:
Join them: read the knob, turn it into an angle with `map()`, and send the servo there.

**Your task:** fill in the blanks.
hints: The servo's angles go from 0 up to what?
The first blank is 180. Then write the angle to the servo.
steps.success: Turn the knob and the servo follows. That's how remote-controlled cars steer!

steps.title: A dashboard gauge
steps.text: **Goal:** the servo only moves when the knob really changes (by more than 2°), and each time it moves, the Serial Monitor shows `Angle: ` and the angle.
hints: Remember the last angle in a variable made above `setup()`.
`abs(angle - lastAngle)` is how far it changed, ignoring plus or minus.
Inside the `if`: write to the servo, print the angle, then set `lastAngle = angle;`.

checks.label: The servo still follows the knob
The Serial Monitor shows the angle when I turn the knob

steps.success: A smooth, quiet gauge. Ignoring tiny changes like this is called a dead band.

outro: Your dial turns a knob into movement, like the needle on a car's dashboard. You read a **potentiometer**, used **map()**, and controlled a **servo** with a library.
stretch: Make the needle move smoothly towards the knob, one degree at a time, instead of jumping.
Add a red LED that lights up when the needle is in the "danger zone" (over 150°).
Make it a speedometer: print a speed from 0 to 120 km/h to the Serial Monitor.
